newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany sees risk of higher budget deficit - report.
newsitem.headline: Germany sees risk of higher budget deficit - report.

text.p: Germany's Der Spiegel weekly magazine said on Saturday Bonn sees a risk of the country's 1997 budget deficit posting a surprising climb beyond levels allowed for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Internal calculations at the Chancellor's office show the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, Der Spiegel said in a release ahead of publication on Monday.

A German government spokesman denied the article, saying the Chancellor's office had not made such calculations, but the report could still unnerve financial markets when trade opens on Monday morning.

The figure is well beyond the three percent level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for joining monetary union and is also above the government's official target of 2.9 percent. The German deficit stood at 3.8 percent last year.

The report could be the latest blow to confidence in Germany's ability to qualify for monetary union. Such a high deficit would mean that even under a liberal interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty Germany would not make the first wave of currency union planned for 1999.
Several Bundesbank council members and leading German economists have expressed scepticism that the country will be able to get its financial house in order in time.
EMU is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999, but the decision as to who can join will be made in the first part of 1998 on the basis of 1997 data.
But far from predicting a postponement or a collapse of EMU, Der Spiegel said Finance Minister Theo Waigel would slash the deficit with changes in budget accounting.

The magazine said Waigel expects to be able to cut the apparent size of the budget deficit by calculating in a 10 billion surplus in pension contributions, eight billion marks from nursing care insurance and 1.75 billion marks in Bundesbank profits.
Government building projects, meanwhile, could be financed privately, allowing the government to delay actual spending beyond this year.

Several members of the Bundesbank council have spoken out against using "accounting tricks" to qualify for monetary union, saying they would threaten confidence in the future European currency, the euro.
